utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. For the Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer present. Before we start, General Pandurevic, news have reached us this morning that your father has passed away. This is a preeminently humanitarian Tribunal, tries to set the example of being humanitarian at all times, and showing how important it is to be humanitarian. We know this is a sad moment for you; and this morning, before we do anything else, we wish to share with you the sorrow you feel and convey to you our condolences, to you and the rest of your family. THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do let us know through your lawyer when you ever the memorial service so we can see what we do about it. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's nice to see you again. We are going to proceed with your examination-in-chief. Mr. Thayer, later on in the week, presumably, we will come down with a scheduling order, and one of the things we are going to make clear and insist in a rigid way is the conclusion of the Prosecution case by the -- by a specific date. So please try to stick to the time that you have indicated for the examination-in-chief and possibly even shorten it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have already shortened it some, and I will do my best to shorten it further. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter number 2986 back up on e-court, please? I'm sorry, 2968. I misspoke. If we may have the second page of each version, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, focusing on the final paragraph of each document, you reported this conversation indicates that General Gvero promised that he would do his utmost to keep the situation in the region of Srebrenica under control, which he thought quite possible because of his competent military there. What happened this day only served to complicate the situation in the region of Srebrenica and would ill effect the situation there. The next sentence reads: "He would have had the full insight into the situation in the Srebrenica area by next morning. That was why he suggested another contact by phone only next morning. He suggested that no air power be used by that time." Sir, at the time that you made these notes, took this report, again, was this the first time that a senior VRS Main Staff officer suggested that you call back or that there be a further future conversation so he could check on the situation, see what was going on with his troops?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not, and by then it was clear to us that it was just -- they are just trying to delay so they could complete the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in this report that you typed up, General Gvero refers to close air support and says, I believe on two occasions in this conversation, according to your notes, your report, that he wants the close air support stopped. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, had a decision at this time, approximately 1810 hours on the 11th, had a decision been made within UNPROFOR about whether or not to end the close air support?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it's mentioned in the first sentence of that document, that the aircrafts were no longer over Srebrenica but they were still at General Gobillard's disposal. So, yes, we had stopped the close air support that had been ongoing earlier that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, sir, was that decision not again to use close air support, was that decision conveyed to the VRS, or was something else conveyed to the VRS in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. That was a terrible question. The final decision not to employ close air support again in connection with the VRS attack on Srebrenica, was that final decision communicated to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was. We had suspended close air support at that time, if I remember correctly, because some Dutch soldiers had been captured by the VRS, and they threatened to kill them if we kept hitting them with close air support, so we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall with any specificity what actual planes were stopped and who in Sarajevo actually gave the order to stop them?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the BH command gave the order and the acting commander at the time was General Gobillard. He may have acted through the Chief of Staff of BH command, who was General Nicolai. I know that two Dutch F-16s had engaged; two Americans F-16s followed, but I'm not sure that they were-- they dropped anything; and A-10s were -- two A-10s were next to come and they were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, just briefly, what type of capabilities does an A-10 have, and do they have anything in particular that's relevant to close air support?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The A-10s are the best aircraft for that kind of air task. They are slower. Their pilots do basically only that, fire on ground support. So they are better trained, and they have a big cannon which is much more accurate. Accuracy, in the case of close air support, is important because the limiting definitions of that type of action usually mean they are being employed in close support to our -- or in close proximity to our own troops. So accuracy is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned some threats to DutchBat peacekeepers. Did you ever learn, during this period of time, about other threats to UN peacekeepers or to civilians which were made on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the VRS advanced, the Dutch withdrew from most of their positions, and they concentrated in the Potocari compound where I guess they had their main base, company base, as well as most of the population of the enclave of Srebrenica that was in the surrounding area. They all fell back in the Potocari compound. At one point, again to stop us from using close air support, the Serbs threatened to shell the compound, with the people in it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to change topics slightly for a moment. Do you recall listening to a radio transmission from Zepa during the VRS attack on that enclave?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had more than one radio communication with Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall a particular transmission which involved a civilian representative from Zepa, speaking over the radio or communications device?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the three civilians that I would later meet in Zepa when I went down there. I believe his name was Horlak. He spoke to us. We were by then back in PTT building in our own headquarters, in the ops room. The Ukrainians had the HF communication with their company in Zepa, and he was using the same equipment that the Ukrainians had at their command post in Zepa to talk to us in the ops room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall with any specificity what this civilian representative that you remember as Mr. Horlak was saying or reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of it right now. I know I have notes of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Are those notes contained in your journal? Is that where?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then what I'd like to do is if we may have 6D00165 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While that's getting loaded up, I think everybody here has heard something about this journal that you kept. Would you just please describe what it is, what it was, and how you created it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every day, while I was in Bosnia, I took notes of important events as they occurred. I also took detailed notes of all the meetings that I attended, most of the time with one of the generals that I was serving, meetings with either the Bosnians, the Serbs, civilians representative, government officials, military officers. Those notes, usually I typed them up the same evening, because as I was saying yesterday, there were meetings more than one usually every day, and I wanted to get this done before I started taking notes again the next day. Also, I had a daily agenda in which I took notes of a more personal nature. So when I got back, when I got back home at the end of the mission, I put together a journal. I wrote a daily paragraph based on my -- that day's page of my diary, and then I cut and paste all the other notes taken in theatre without altering them. Basically, I just cut and paste them into the chronological order of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what did you do with your original notes, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dumped most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may turn to page 127 of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From what you observed and what you learned, what were some of the challenges that Colonel Verhoglyad faced as -- in his command, and how did he respond to some of those challenges, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that particular Ukrainian Battalion was certainly not of the best quality of soldiers, from my understanding. From many discussions with Colonel Verhoglyad was that they were all volunteers and basically fleeing their own country because they were in trouble back there. So lots of discipline problems both in the enclaves where they were, but more so in Sarajevo and in still barracks with the Ukrainians soldiers there. Colonel Verhoglyad, of course, wanted to change that perception because the French, who consisted more than half of the troops, and headquarters of the sector did not pay too much attention or give too much credit to the Ukrainians, of course. Colonel Verhoglyad wanted to change that. He first, I believe, had to convince his own national headquarters to provide better troops, better equipment, and he did quite a bit of work to come up with a better contribution in time for IFOR, when there was a transfer of authority to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear any reports or rumours about the Ukrainians either in the Zepa enclave or elsewhere, the peacekeepers, being involved in any improper trade with anyone?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories about high usage of fuel. They had nowhere to go basically, and their fuel usage was higher than units who were patrolling in other areas. So we suspected, we knew, Colonel Verhoglyad knew, that they were trading that fuel with the Serbs for, I don't really know what. This became annoying because we had problems resupplying our own troops in the various enclaves, and fuel was a major commodity.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall at all when these reports of trading fuel were supposed to have occurred? Do you recall whether it was before you arrived, during your time there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything specific. All I can say is that these facts came to my knowledge at about the same time as we were paying attention to them in Zepa and Gorazde, so when those events started occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever hear any complaints or any information about the Ukrainian peacekeepers being partial to one side or the other? Did you ever hear any talk of that as well?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was discussed, mostly among the French, that the Ukrainians were pro-Serb. They could more easily leave -- live on the Serb side than anyone else. In fact, after the hostage crisis in May, we had orders that no UNPROFOR soldiers were to go in Serb territory, and that order lasted for many weeks. However, we still needed to keep in touch around Sarajevo with the Serb liaison officer, and we used the Ukrainians to do that because they could travel back and forth and not be made hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may look at 65 ter number 2502, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we looked at a couple of these during your proofing session, and to save time I'm just going to show you one. Do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a report prepared by David Harland who was a civil affairs officer at the sector level.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I note for the record that it's the 15th of July 1995, and it's headed, "Sector Sarajevo, Weekly Situation Report." Colonel, would you regularly receive these weekly sit-reps in the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were addressed to the sector commander, as you see in the internal distribution; and, basically, all operational reporting or UN paper work that went to the commander first went through me. So I saw most of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so you would review them, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that correct? Okay. And if you would share with the Court, Colonel, how useful or not useful did you find Harland's reporting?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I find them useful in that he was good at gathering information from various sources and putting it all together. And in the diary, I sometimes -- I know early on I talked about the use of the military observers, which knew a lot of stuff, but it was not very well integrated into how we processed that information at the sector level. Let's just say that the proper staffing reflections were not concerned, most of the time as they concerned UNMOs. But David would always get the information: The information from the UNMOs, the UNHCR who had convoys everywhere, from himself or his travels, or other civil affairs officers who were on the ground who had a different perspective. So those -- I found those reports usually normally accurate but enlightening, in that his sources were wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at page 2 of the English and we'll stay on page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When we met, you told me you couldn't recall all the information in -- regarding Zepa in this report. I just want to ask you about a couple of sections in it. If we could go to the -- or if I could direct your attention to the paragraph that begins, "Last Saturday."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Any time you need to go into private session, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "Last Saturday, 8 July, the Bosnians asked UNPROFOR to return the 127 weapons that had been handed over to UNPROFOR following the demilitarisation agreement of May -- or of 8 May 1993." Sir, do you recall receiving any reports or information concerning the Bosnians attempts to get back or retrieve weapons that had been handed over?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we had weapons collection point in most of the enclaves, including Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, on both sides. Both factions had to put their heavy weapons in weapon collection point. Those are the weapons that are being talked about, and the Bosnians wanted to have those weapons to defends themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go -- if I could just focus your attention on the very last sentence of the very last paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This would be, on the B/C/S version, the third full paragraph that appears on the B/C/S side, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "On the same day, the commander of Bosnian forces in the pocket threatened to kill UNPROFOR soldiers if they did nothing to help defend the pocket." Colonel, what information do you recall receiving, if any, about the Ukrainian company being threatened or actually attacked by either of the warring parties during the attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, they had, as I started to describe earlier, they had OPs around the enclaves and they had their check-point at the top of the road, check-point 2, and they had a command post down in the village. Some of the OPs were blocked by the Serbs to prevent them from going anywhere. Some were blocked by the Bosnians with attempt by the Bosnians to get the weapons and the equipment that the Ukrainians had. There was a pressure by the Bosnians on the Ukrainians at their command post in the village, to give them all the weapons, one-quarter of their ammunition. So they were pressured on both sides. Of course, as we saw earlier in the discussion with Mr. Horlak, they were putting a lot of pressure for us to do something, to either give them weapons or provide close air support to stop the Serb attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And having reviewed this particular report by David Harland, do you have any reason to doubt its accuracy or truthfulness of the information contained in it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sticking with the topic of the attack on Zepa, Colonel, do you recall what role, if any, NATO aircraft played during the VRS attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had air presence, as it is called, at one -- at one point, but we did not use the aircraft neither close air support or air strikes for a number of reasons. The situation on the ground was confused, and the -- similar to the situation we were talking about in Srebrenica yesterday. Also, the Ukrainians did not have a tactical air command post present to direct -- to talk to the air planes and direct their fire on the ground. It is essential to make sure that bombs fall where they are supposed to. So that was, in my view, the major military hurdle to using close air support in the case of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, even though there was no actual close air support employed in connection with the VRS attack on Zepa, were there any consequences to the actual air presence over Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't like it, and that was relayed to us. I remember that, but I don't remember the details of their reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, before we go to your diary --?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's just go into private session, if we could, Mr. President, straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when you personally went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe how that came to pass, please?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we decided -- it happened about ten days later, around the 26th of July; and this, what we just saw, had been ongoing for those further ten days. We decided to reinforce the Ukrainians in Zepa; and since we could not prevent the Serbs from reducing that pocket, we were going to make sure that the population was looked after and evacuated safely. So we decided to reinforce the Ukrainians by sending French and Russian troops. General Gobillard, the best means of communications to keep in touch with either BH command, the force commander, the people in the pocket, and all the procedural around the use of aircrafts and things like that, he felt he had to stay at PTT. So he sent me to be his eyes and ears to Zepa, in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the movement of the civilian population out of the Zepa enclave, Colonel, by the 26th, when you were sent down there, what's your understanding of what had already happened?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the evacuation started before I got there. What we wanted to do is make sure that each bus or vehicle carrying evacuees out of Zepa to Kladanj in Bosnian territory, which is where they were supposed to be evacuated, that each bus or vehicle was to have one UN soldier on board. Basically, the task of those soldiers was to make sure that the vehicle got to Kladanj, and that nobody was pulled off the vehicle by the Serbs on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was that an objective?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without having all the details of what had happened to the Srebrenica 15 days earlier, we knew, we had information that many thousands Bosnian males had disappeared and have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall specifically with whom you travelled to Zepa on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled with Colonel Chinouihl. He was the senior French engineer on staff at headquarters Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you make it to Zepa straight away, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. We got stopped at every Serb check-point on the way; and when we got to Rogatica, we were stopped there for 18 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, do you recall seeing or doing while you were at Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we attempted to -- every time we saw an opportunity to just drive through, obtain authority to carry on to Zepa, negotiate, argue, and try to move out of there, at one point we saw buses and other vehicles driving in the opposite direction, full of Bosnian evacuates from Zepa. We entered that they had a soldier on board, most did. At one point, we saw a dump truck with nobody, with no UN soldier and about 50 people sitting on the metal bed of the dump truck with a big tarp over them. It was probably -- that was in July. It was probably close to 50 degrees in the back of -- in the back of that dumptruck. When we didn't see any UN soldiers there, we basically stood in front of the vehicle. Colonel Chinouihl took the initiative and stood right in front of the vehicle and I joined them, and we said, "This vehicle is not going anywhere until we have a UN soldier to put on board." They got excited, cocked their weapon, and threatened us, Chinouihl and I. And, eventually, we saw -- eventually they calmed down and they agreed to what we were saying. We got the people off the truck, to take a bit of fresh air; and, eventually, a bus returning with four or five Ukrainian soldiers from Kladanj drove by and we got one, and we told him to get on the truck and make sure that it made its way to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Were the passengers male, female, or mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mixed, but mostly very young and very old, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe, sir, what, if anything, you did to help any of those elderly people off the dumptruck?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- I remember this very old lady, and it was really hot in the back of that truck. It was hot outside, hot and humid, and even more so in the back of that truck. She had trouble, basically, unfolding her legs to be able to walk off the truck, so we helped her off, helped her to walk a little bit and get some air. That's the one thing I remember in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you spend that night, sir, the night of the 26th?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, other than that episode, it was at night-time in the evening, we slept in our vehicles. I was personally in a small French armoured vehicle. A very cramped space, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That brings us to the 27th. What did you do that day?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, eventually, we were let through. We drove to Zepa and not to the village but to the check-point on top of the hill, which was, as I said, probably a kilometre or a kilometre and a half from the village, where we met other UN troops that had been sent, as well as people being evacuated and Serbs getting about their business of evacuating those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at this check-point, did you meet or speak with any UN officers in particular?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Chinouihl and I went to -- we found Colonel Germain the Colonel Germain who was a French legionnaire, who had been sent there along with the Russians reinforcements, and we asked him about what was going on, what was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he had been in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do and what did you see while you were there at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I got there, I remember the people. The road coming from the village was a one-way road attached to the side of a cliff basically going up, and so trucks would come up to the large parking area, check-point 2, unload the Bosnian civilians that they had taken from the village. They would be transferred to buses, and those buses would then go to Kladanj. There were mostly old people or young kids with their mothers, and it was a bit - how should I put it? - unreal feeling to see that. These people were basically forcibly removed from their house, trying to keep their family together. I saw a young mother with two kids trying to keep them together and move on the bus, and a Serb soldier prodding her along, most of the time without any emotion, but in some cases with screaming. And all those UN soldiers were around watching it, basically with arms along their side, having abandoned -- nobody did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned screaming, sir. Who was screaming?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one Serb basically clowning around. He had -- I guess he felt very powerful in the middle of it all, and he was clowning around and screaming at people, "Get on the bus, move faster," at least I assume that's what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe the condition of these civilians that you saw? Take your time and describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were sad, of course, but -- in fact, they were emotionless. They were -- we knew they were being forced to leave everything behind, and they had to go basically with the clothes they were wearing and that's it. They were, as we say in French, "resignes avec leur sort."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, roughly, what does that mean? My French is pretty elementary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's "reconciled with their destiny." Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or with their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did you see General Mladic at this check-point at some point?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there. In fact, shortly after our arrival, Colonel Germain told Chinouihl and I that Mladic had been meeting with three civilian representatives from the Bosnian of Zepa and that he was about to meet again with them. So we asked one Serb soldier to find us room -- or, no, to be able to attend that meeting, and he went and talked to the individual. I don't know who it was at the time. The individual came back and he said, "You," pointing at me, "Can come with an interpreter." I was travelling with a French legionnaire soldier of Slovenian origin. So he and I went and attended the meeting, and the person who had been approached and said, "Yes, the Canadian can come," was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went and sat down. He showed me where to sit beside him, to attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- it didn't start right away. The three Bosnian representatives were brought to the meeting place. They seemed in decent enough shape. They didn't seem to have been mistreated or anything, a bit unsecure, probably, but nothing else that I could see. It didn't start right away. But when it started, it didn't seem to be an agenda. It was more like, "Are we going to sign that agreement," something they had discussed before, I guess; and then veiled threats, which I don't remember the details, but basically that he didn't need all three of them to reach that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "he," who are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those representatives or their faces?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one, Horlak or Torlak, who I mentioned earlier, that I recognised his face; the others, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may look at some video very, very briefly, without referring to any particular date, I just want to see whether you recognise any faces, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are going to be looking at P02489.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are just going to play a very brief clip, and I'll ask you if you recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, anybody in that clip, which started at approximately 12 minutes 7 seconds and we paused at 12 minutes 15.9 seconds, is there anybody you recognise there as a civilian representative that you met during your time in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the one with the white shirt who is shaking hands with Mladic, the last one shaking hands with him, is the one I recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the short sleeve shirt, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are going to play another clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 2491. We are going to start the clip at 46 minutes and 6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we have paused the frame at 46 minutes, 12.3 seconds. Do you recognise anyone in this clip?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the left, I see Lieutenant-Colonel Germain, French legionnaire. Facing us is Lieutenant-Colonel Jim Baxter who was the military assistant to General Smith. On his right is General Rupert Smith who was commander UNPROFOR at the time and who joined me at that meeting we were just talking about shortly after it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record, the individual that you've referred to as Lieutenant-Colonel Germain is the individual without the beard to the left of the frame; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we continue rolling the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've paused at 46 minutes, 25.4 seconds. Do you recognise anyone in this clip, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the one we see, the closest, is Mladic. Behind him with the mustache is Indic. He was the one who was our main contact or liaison officer with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that would be Lieutenant-Colonel Indic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are done with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please summarise briefly what you occur happening during the rest of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, shortly after it started, General Smith arrived and he joined the meeting, and then Mladic was trying to get the Bosnian to sign an agreement. However, UNPROFOR had many guarantees to provide in that agreement and guarantees we could not provide. So General Smith intervened and took the three Bosnian civilian representatives aside to tell them, "Don't sign that because we can't offer the guarantees that Mladic says that we can offer, so you will sign without those UNPROFOR guarantees." He also told Mladic that these people were local representatives. They were not representatives of the Bosnian government. Basically, one of the aspects of that -- of the agreement relied on an eventual exchange of prisoners, which needed to be negotiated at much higher level. So these people could not agree to some of the things Mladic was asking them to agree to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After this meeting, what do you recall doing next? Did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, Mladic drove down to Zepa village, and I followed with Lieutenant-Colonel Germain. I went down to the Ukrainian command post in the village where they were set up, and that's where I met Colonel Verhoglyad who was already there, the Ukrainian deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you see going on down in the village centre there, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Serb soldiers, not the most clean-cut types. I guess they had been fighting, or you know, for a while, evacuating or looting. I saw trucks go by with fridges, with cows in the back. I guess they were going around the houses and taking whatever was worth taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How would you describe the looting that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- there were a few houses on fire, not -- there was a kind of a central place where I was. There were no fires nearby. But further down, I could see houses burning, and I heard the occasional shot in the background, weapon being fired. And at one point, I'm not sure if it's that same day, I believe so, Mladic with his camera crew was trying to offer water to an old lady who was sitting on the stairs of a big building there. They were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of the 27th of July, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the Ukrainian compound in Zepa village. I guess it was a school that they were using for their rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That brings us to the 28th. Do you recall what you saw going on in the village that morning?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember, I'm not sure if what I saw was the afternoon before or the morning after, more of the same. There were still Serb soldiers there, and I walked around with the interpreter that I had, the French legionnaire, and we talked to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were those Serb soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific at that point, because they were -- the evacuation of the village itself was completed, I believe, at that time; although, I can't say the same about the whole enclave. No, there was the looting still, and grabbing whatever they could, putting it on trucks. One of them wanted to see my gun, so I showed him after making the proper safety procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to an old woman that you encountered. Can you just describe -- describe that encounter and describe what, if anything, you did in connection with her?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the old woman that Mladic had been offering, I think, water and chocolate to her, in front of his camera crew. It was a show of poor taste any way. After that episode, we took her - "we" being the my interpreter and I - we took her to the Ukrainian compound. She didn't want to go. She was very scared, but we finally convinced her not to stay in the village. We wanted her to -- we wanted her to rest, to give her something to eat, and she didn't want to go into the school, the building that the Ukrainians were using. So we -- I got some soldiers to get a mattress inside, take it outside under the shade of a tree, so that she could sit down. There was an old man who had been old, in relative terms. He might have been 50 to 60 and who already was in the Ukrainian compound. So we asked him to come out and help us convince her that she was safer there and to stay there, which he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what arrangements did you make, in connection with these two people, for their transportation?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to leave shortly after, but I made sure that the Ukrainians knew that they had to take these people out and that they should be evacuated properly and not be left on their own; and by then, because Verhoglyad was there, I trusted that they would do that job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you do later in the day?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove back up to check-point 2, and that's where we met General Gobillard, who had travelled to Zepa that day; and then after meeting there, we travelled back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while you were with General Gobillard at check-point 2, did you have any meetings with any VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know I have some notes, but I don't remember the -- that part very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And before we get to the notes, do you remember who the meeting was with?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see you shaking your head, so we'll go to the document straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 2969 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want this in open?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Open session is fine, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could zoom out a little bit on the English, just to get the full. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you read that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a report of that meeting that I personally wrote. It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who is this meeting with, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And General Gobillard who had travelled to Zepa that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we read the header line, the underlined portion, can you just read what that says, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Meeting, General Gobillard, Tolimir, Zepa Ukrainian check-point 2, 28 July 95 at 1720."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, just take a couple of moments to read this first page.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At paragraph 1(A), you indicate that one of the things that was discussed, one of the matters discussed was the reasons for taking 36 Bosnian civilians from the last two convoys on the evening of 27 July and for taking one other Bosnian civilian at check-point 2 on the afternoon of 28 July. Sir, do you recall who had this information about the 36 Bosnian civilians and the one Bosnian civilian at check-point 2?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Gobillard had that information. I don't know where from, because I drove up from Zepa village to check-point 2 at that day to meet him there and I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page to page 2 in the English, please, and that will also have to be page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the top of the English, you write that: "General Tolimir explained that these civilians were, in fact, males of military age, 18 to 60, and that they had lied about their age to try to escape from Zepa. This included the 12 slightly wounded." Do you recall hearing any information about these 12 slightly wounded?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not entirely sober, and it seemed to be a usual state for him, according to General Gobillard at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I see we are at the break time. I only have about five minutes left of my examination in chief, so we'll pick up when we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break. Let's have the break. But whoever is going first with the cross-examination, please be prepared. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got your five minutes, Mr. Thayer. I see that you are going to make it ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I wanted to follow up with a question about the video clip that I showed you previously. You identified one of the Muslim representatives you recalled as wearing the white short sleeved shirt. Is there a name that you associate with that individual in the short sleeved shirt?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Horlak or Torlak. I'm not sure the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were in Zepa, do you recall seeing any other VRS officers of any rank other than Generals Mladic and Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the name Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who do you recall him being?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Bosnian military leader of whatever troops the BiH army had in the Zepa pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing him during your time in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we were looking at some notes you took of your meeting with General Tolimir and General Gobillard. What did you eventually do with those notes, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- whenever I drafted notes quickly like that in handwriting, it meant they had to go. So BH command definitely got a copy and probably the force commander's office as well in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when do you recall finalising the -- those notes?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as usual, as soon as we got back to the office, I would get into doing this; and in this case, the fact that they are handwritten tells me that it happened fast, that we needed to share that information very quickly. Otherwise, I would have waited later at night and typed them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when do you recall returning to Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime on the 28th, I believe, after that meeting with Tolimir at check-point 2, I think we headed back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever return to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 2969 back up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may go to page 3 of the English, and that is page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want this in public, in open session, or in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Public session is fine, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we go towards the bottom -- middle to the bottom of the English, and we will be focusing on about the lower third of paragraph 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just quickly, there is a reference, and you write, you report: "As for the Bosnian military, it seems that they are ready and willing to drop their weapons and surrender provided that they obtain firm guarantees for their safety from UNPROFOR." Do you remember where you got that information from, sir, to include in these notes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, and we can stay on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please focus your attention on the passage that begins with the word, "Note." "Shortly after General Gobillard's departure, the Serbs took Mr. Mehmet Hanic, mayor and leader of the War Presidency of Zepa, under custody since they didn't need him any more and he is of military age. They had been using him as a mediator with the people of Zepa. It is believed that Mr. Hajric honestly and courageously did his best to save his people." Now, do you recall taking this note, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you explain how something that happened after you left made it into your note? Do you know what the source of this information was?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact source, but I remember how these things happened. I would put, as a note, something that I learned in between the time of the meeting and the time that the actual transcript was produced. If it was pertinent to that meeting or to that report, I would add it as a note, like this. It's probably on returning to Sarajevo, to sector headquarters, that I got this information, either from the ops room or perhaps from Mr. David Harland, who was in touch with the civil affairs officer who was still at Zepa when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that civil affairs officer, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been Ed Joseph or Viktor Bezrouchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you know or did you receive any information as to whether Mr. Hajric was ever seen alive again?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that needs to be clarified. You don't know what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had that kind of information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we just look at paragraph 5, if we just scroll down a bit, and this is also paragraph 5 in the corresponding B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "General Tolimir suggested that since UNPROFOR had accomplished its task of evacuating the civilians, and since it was not willing to help with the Bosnian military, it should withdraw." Do you recall where this information came from, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're reporting what Tolimir actually said during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may turn to the last page of the English, please? That would be page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This refers to the whereabouts of Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "General Gobillard asked if it was true, as General Mladic had said, that Palic was dead. "Tolimir announced," General Tolimir announced, "that like every army they used propaganda to affect the morale of its enemy and that this information that he could not confirm himself was probably such propaganda." Do you know where General Gobillard got that information about Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, when he got to check-point 2, on the top there of the hill at Zepa. I was still down in the village, so he probably talked to some of the officers, UN officers, who were there and got that information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever learn what Colonel Palic's fate was, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, there is some initials here at the bottom of the page. Can you identify those?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Let's go through the estimated time for cross-examinations once more. So far, it's only the Pandurevic team that does not intend to cross-examine this witness. Do I have a confirmation of that, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Zivanovic, you asked for 30 minutes. Do you still need the 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, you asked for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. About 45 minutes to an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Ms. Nikolic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, you had asked for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It is very unlikely that we will have any cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Madam Fauveau, you had asked for an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you stick to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll try to be as short as possible and be finished in an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, you had asked for two hours -- a revised estimate for two hours and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly no more than that, and I hope perhaps to cut it down to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So that gives you an idea that it's very unlikely that you finish your testimony today, but that you will certainly finish it tomorrow. Madam Fauveau, I gather that you are going first. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my name is Natacha Fauveau-Ivanovic representing General Miletic. So, first, let's look at your statement with the OTP in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document 6D152. Could we please show page 3 to the witness, at the bottom of the page. I need the bottom of page 3 and page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, in this statement, you were talking about the meetings held with the different commands of UNPROFOR; and on the third line, from the bottom of the page, you say and I quote: [In English] "This meeting with the BH command MA Serb, a very important function, they ensured the link between the sector and BH command was operating smoothly. I and the other MAs would use these sessions to ensure that Generals..."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "... that Generals Smith and Gobillard, as well as Gobillard's successors, fully understood one another. There was important given the different languages and cultural and military differences in perception and reactions." [Interpretation] So what I'm interested in is the last sentence. You're talking about different languages, cultural, and military differences in perception and reactions. Does this mean that each officer saw and analysed the situation according to what he knew in his own environment, so according to his own military experience?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. That's why we had those sessions to make sure that this didn't happen, and we had -- they had sessions to get –

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Sorry to interrupt you like this. But Madam Fauveau and Mr. Thayer and you, Major, please draw our attention straight away when we need to be in private session. I'm not quite sure whether this part should be in open or in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the OTP agrees to have this in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But draw our attention straight away when you think that we should be in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So I understand that you had meetings to make sure that there was coherence. But if there had been no meetings of the like, wouldn't it be that each officer would analyse the situation according to his own background and his own experience?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but that doesn't mean that they would be different. Lack of meetings did not necessarily mean lack of coherence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But since there were officers that came from all different countries and had different cultural backgrounds, and who came from different armies, I'm not talking about coherence that may or may not exist; I'm talking about the fact that all these UNPROFOR officers had different backgrounds. So is it true that they all had different habits, they all had different ways of operating within an army?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. They were all NATO trained, including the French who were trained on NATO procedures. So we had that common background: Dutch, British, French, and Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What about the Ukrainians, or the Egyptians?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't have that common background of NATO training.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement, you talk about the way your sector was organised, and you say that the commander of the sector had three deputy commanders and the head of staff right below him. What exactly was the hierarchical connection between these four people?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- the three deputies were at the same level, and they accomplished similar functions for their own national contingent. The Chief of Staff, who was Russian, had similar functions toward his national contingents, as the other deputies did, but he was also running the headquarters staff for the general.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who replaced General Gobillard when he was not in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on who was present, there was often absence for either leave back home or meeting elsewhere. It was in descending order, the deputies, which were given a seniority before I got there: The Egyptian deputy was the senior, then the Ukrainian, and finally the French.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was the head of General Gobillard's staff?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Russian.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the name of General Miletic was a name you heard in July 1995. Do you remember this? On page 95, you said this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also said, on page 82, that during the Srebrenica events, you spent a great amount of time in the UNPROFOR HQ because General Gobillard was the acting commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Gobillard was acting commander, he had contacts with the officers in charge, the higher officers of Republika Srpska army, right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you have no recollection that at the time, in July 1995, General Gobillard had contacts with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I'd have no -- I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you have no recollection that General Nicolai would have had contacts with General Miletic over that same period, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you have no recollection that -- of the name of General Miletic being mentioned during the meetings you had in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, and I know I have something on him in my notes. But off the top of my head, I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness a document 5D532?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is information provided by the OTP after the meeting you had with representatives of the OTP last Sunday. Could you please read this first paragraph, but just for yourself.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that during this meeting two days ago, on Sunday, November 25th, you told the Prosecutor that you believed you heard about Miletic in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You earlier you said that in your notes you believe you have something about Miletic, but it's not this September meeting. It's not this meeting of September 24, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It likely is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I apologise. I was talking about the meeting of November 24, 1995.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both -- both of those meetings appear in my notes. I did not attend the first one, but I attended the other one, and I don't really remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 81, you said that you were not really sure of the duties of General Miletic, but you said that he was a deputy to commander Mladic, as well as probably head of the intelligence or the security sector. Isn't it true that when you were saying this, you were just assuming that it was the truth, but, in fact, you never really knew what the exact function of General Miletic was?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I knew is that he was a senior officer in the VRS army, above corps level, so in General Mladic's staff, but I did not know his exact function.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true that when you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina in May 1995, there was an ABiH offensive ongoing?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This offensive was led from demilitarised zone, including Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Serbs reacted to this offensive, they were given an ultimatum to stop their response against the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be helpful to have a date or something to tie this down to the actual events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. I think that's a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness document 6D152, the statement he made with the OTP, page 10, third paragraph. I quote: [In English] "In response to the Bosnian attack, the Bosnian Serbs started to fire their weapons which had been gathered in the WCPs. The sector issued an ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs to stop firing and to return their weapons to the WCPs by noon on May 25, 1995." [Interpretation] I believe that this answers the question from my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that when the Serbs responded to the Bosnian attack, they were issued an ultimatum from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a larger context here. Weapons in WCPs are heavy weapons, which were collected under UNPROFOR supervision in weapon collection points. Those are the weapons that the Serbs were using that we didn't want them to use; and, also, they strangled the city and the city was starving. So that's one reason why we tried to negotiate more food into the city and the Bosnians tried fighting their way out with light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Fine. I'm not contesting this right now. But before the Bosnian Serbs responded, the Muslims did attack from a zone that was supposed to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I was alluding to, "demilitarise" meant having heavy weapons under UN supervision in weapon collection points, not all types of weapons. It was impossible to do, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But in this offensive that started from Sarajevo, the ABiH army, and within Sarajevo also, within the DMZ zone, the ABiH was also using heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time, no. Eventually, everybody was using their heavy weapons because weapon collection point ceased to exist, but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true that at the moment, during this offensive, the representative of the ABiH, General Delic, for example, did not want to speak about peace?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please -- I think here we need to go into private session because this is document 6D165. It's the diary, the journal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a memo dated July 2nd, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to page 3, please? The two last paragraphs are the ones I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the whole text. It's too narrow. Good.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the paragraph right under the heading, "Location of Bosnian weapons a problem," there is the following: [In English] "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago, the number of Bosnian heavy weapons operating from near UNPROFOR facilities has significantly increased." [Interpretation] So early in July 1995, didn't the ABiH army operate with heavy weapons out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, as I pointed out earlier, between May, your initial questions, and July, the big change was the WCPs were not functional any more, so everyone was using heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But when these WCPs no longer operated, didn't it mean that the DMZ was also no longer operational?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that in June 1995, the UNPROFOR had many problems with the ABiH army? At the time, notably the ABiH army was restricting the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we need to move into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a cable sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the stamp, at the top of the page...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: ... it says: "95, July 11, 2147 hours."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: 2147. Does this mean that the cable was sent at 2147 hours?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fair assumption. The stamp is UNPROFOR communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: See paragraph B in this document? In the middle of this document, there is a sentence starting with, "Following." In this part of the cable, it reads as follows: [In English] "Following consultation with the Bosnian government, and in order to avoid a continued humanitarian catastrophe, agreement will be solicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica, including all men, to leave for Tuzla if they so wish. "The Dutch will be instructed to remain in the Srebrenica enclave at least until arrangements have been negotiated and finalised with Bosnian Serbs authorities for the departure from the enclave of those people." [Interpretation] Could we say that this cable was a follow-up of the contact that Mr. Akashi had had with the people at the UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, amongst many other contacts he must have had in times of crises like that. We never stopped discussing, gathering information, exchanging ideas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this cable, the UNPROFOR was supposed to ask the Serbs for help in order to evacuate the population, the Muslim population, from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "agreement to allow all residents of Srebrenica to leave for Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. In any case, the initiative calling for evacuation came from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that point, after three or four days of Serb pressure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And as follow-up, after all these contacts that UNPROFOR had with the BiH government, as well as with Mr. Akashi, the commander of DutchBat held a meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, I want to know whether a meeting was actually organised on the evening of the 11th between the commander of the DutchBat and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you --?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please first go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 5D165 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this was discussed; but by whom exactly, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Zepa was supposed to be demilitarised in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Anything that happened prior to May 1995, which was arrival, I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember that when -- according to the information you obtained, do you remember that when Tolimir received this suggestion that Zepa be demilitarised, July 1995, that he seemed to be interested by this proposal?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now move to private session, because I would like to show the witness his diary, 6D155 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that when the evacuation of the population, civilian population, of Zepa was finished, General Tolimir proposed to you to go and see -- that the UNPROFOR should go and see in the forests around whether there were still people who needed to be evacuated? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the meeting General Gobillard held with General Tolimir at check-point 2, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't recall that specifically, but it's possible. There was one thing at that point that was -- that was unsure. We estimated that there were three -- 2.000 to 3.000 people remaining in Zepa at that time. According to the Serbs, they were all BiH army. According to us, at least half were civilians, but we were unsure of those figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like now to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, also, because you speak the same language, please allow a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, again, my name is John Ostojic. I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara. I'd like to ask you some preliminary questions. First, if you will, list for me the documents that you reviewed with the Prosecutor in preparation for your testimony here yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of my diary; the notes of the meeting that I had prepared following the conversation on the phone between General Gobillard and Gvero; notes of another meeting -- yes, notes of the meeting between General Gobillard and General Tolimir at check-point 2 in Zepa; and a report, the weekly report, that David Harland wrote on 2nd of July 1995 that we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is that situation report we referred to?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a weekly report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Oh, the weekly report. Did you review any situation reports?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other than reports that are in my diary, which we've been through some parts of, and there are situation reports in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned with Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please make pauses. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned, with respect to Mr. Harland and his weekly report, that you found it to be useful and reliable. Did you find that to be true for the situation reports that you received on a daily basis from the various organisations that were providing information to you in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not always. This is, how to say, the various sources of information that we had provided us with information that was accurate from their perspective, from their point of view, but not necessarily a complete picture of what was going on.
